newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court allows suspension without hearing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court allows suspension without hearing.

text.p: A unanimous Supreme Court ruled Monday that a state agency was not required to provide notice and a hearing before suspending a public employee without pay.

Justice Antonin Scalia said for the court in the 11-page opinion that the constitutional guarantee of due process under the law does not require a hearing in such cases, especially when they involve criminal charges.

"The government does not have to give an employee charged with a felony a paid leave at taxpayer expense," he said. "The Constitution does not require the government to bear the added expense of hiring a replacement while still paying him."

The case involved Richard Homar, a police officer at East Stroudsburg University in Pennsylvania who was suspended in 1992 after his arrest on drug charges. He was suspended without pay, effective immediately.
The justices overturned a U.S. appeals court ruling that the Homar was constitutionally entitled to a hearing to know the evidence against him and to have a chance to respond.
Scalia said the state has a significant interest in immediately suspending employees who face criminal charges and occupy positions of public trust or visibility, such as police officers.
He said the rights of the employees were properly protected as long as they receive a "sufficiently prompt" hearing after their suspension.
